Hi -- read Ree & Smith (2008), Systematic Biology.  Their "M3" model is a time-stratified model.  Time-stratification allows the geography to change in different time periods.

For example, a researcher might want the areas, distances, and/or dispersal multipliers, etc. to be different in each time bin. 

The borders between time-bins are specified in millions-of-years, in the timeperiods file.

Example files are here:
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#files

Cheers, Nick

Hi!  If you have 2 areas, A and B, then you have 4 ranges:

Null, A, B, and AB

Each range is a state, so you have 4 states. In likelihood models we talk about the state space a lot. Eg for a binary character there are 2 states, 0 and 1. For DNA there are 4 states, A,C,G,T.

Computer analyses get slow above 1000 states, which is 10 areas (2^10=1024), so you can use numstates_from_numareas() to help plan your analysis.

Cheers! Nick
